lessons.plain: A functional dependency is a promise about the data: once you know the values on the left, the values on the right are fixed. Closure helps test keys and consequences.
goals: Read X → Y as a rule about rows
Use closure to find keys and check dependency sets

topics.title: Functional dependency
topics.definition: X → Y means that any two rows with the same X values must also have the same Y values.
details: It is a rule the organization promises to follow, not just a pattern noticed in a small sample.
X is the determinant. Y is determined by X. If a student id identifies a student, sid → name.
topics.example: If course id determines the department, then two rows with the same cid must have the same department.

topics.title: Attribute closure
topics.definition: X⁺ is the set of all attributes that the dependency rules can determine from X.
details: Start with X. Whenever the left side of a dependency is already in the set, add its right side. Repeat until no new attribute can be added.
If X⁺ contains every attribute of the relation, X is a superkey. If no smaller subset works, it is a candidate key.
topics.example: Let R(A,B,C,D) have FDs A→B, B→C, and AC→D. Start A+={A}; A→B adds B; B→C adds C; now AC→D adds D. Thus A+={A,B,C,D}; A is a superkey and is a candidate key if no proper subset determines every column.

topics.title: Armstrong rules and minimal cover
topics.definition: Armstrong's reflexivity, augmentation, and transitivity rules derive dependencies that logically follow from the original rules.
details: Reflexivity: if Y is contained in X, then X → Y. Augmentation: if X → Y, then XZ → YZ. Transitivity: if X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z.
A minimal (canonical) cover has one attribute on each right side, no unnecessary left-side attributes, and no redundant dependency.
topics.example: If sid → name and name → email, then sid → email by transitivity.

worked.title: Find the key of a course-enrollment relation
worked.setup: R(Student, Course, Grade, Instructor, Room). Rules: Student,Course → Grade; Course → Instructor; Instructor → Room.

steps.title: Begin with the proposed key
steps.body: Start closure of {Student, Course}: it currently contains Student and Course.

steps.title: Apply the matching rules
steps.body: Student,Course → Grade adds Grade. Course → Instructor adds Instructor. Instructor → Room adds Room.

steps.title: Check all attributes and minimality
steps.body: The closure now contains Student, Course, Grade, Instructor, and Room, so the pair is a superkey. Neither Student alone nor Course alone determines every attribute, so the pair is a candidate key.

worked.answer: {Student, Course}⁺ contains every attribute. The candidate key is {Student, Course}.

diagram.title: Closure grows as rules are applied
diagram.caption: Keep applying any rule whose left-hand side is already known.

lessons.exam: Compute closures and candidate keys. State Armstrong's axioms and find a canonical cover for a small FD set.

lessons.plain: Schema refinement uses keys and functional dependencies to reduce repeated facts and anomalies. Normal forms guide the design, while decomposition checks protect meaning and rules.
goals: Find update, insertion, and deletion anomalies
Follow a refinement workflow using keys and dependencies

topics.title: Why redundancy causes anomalies
topics.definition: Redundancy is storing the same fact repeatedly. An anomaly is an error or awkwardness caused by that repetition.
details: Update anomaly: some copies change and others do not. Insert anomaly: a fact cannot be stored without an unrelated fact. Delete anomaly: removing one row accidentally removes another fact.
Normalization uses keys and dependencies to decide which facts belong together.
topics.example: If a course title appears on every enrollment row, a title correction must be applied to every student taking that course.

topics.title: Schema refinement in database design
topics.definition: Schema refinement improves a table design so each fact is stored in an appropriate place and common changes do not cause anomalies.
details: Start from requirements. Identify candidate keys and functional dependencies; use them to see which attributes depend on which facts.
Decompose a relation when repeated facts create update, insertion, or deletion anomalies. Select a normal form, then check losslessness and dependency preservation.
A good refinement preserves meaning. Splitting tables without checking their joins can create false combinations or make rules difficult to enforce.
topics.example: For ENROLLMENT(sid,studentName,cid,courseTitle,grade), sid→studentName, cid→courseTitle, and (sid,cid)→grade. Refine into STUDENT(sid,studentName), COURSE(cid,courseTitle), and ENROLLMENT(sid,cid,grade).

topics.title: First and second normal form
topics.definition: 1NF requires each cell to hold one value for its chosen domain. 2NF requires 1NF and no non-key attribute to depend on only part of a composite candidate key.
details: A repeating list of phone numbers in one cell violates the intended atomic layout; store one phone per row or in a separate relation.
Partial dependency matters only when a candidate key has multiple attributes. A student's name depends on sid, not on the full (sid,cid) enrollment key.
topics.example: For key (sid,cid), sid → sname is a partial dependency. Put the name in STUDENT(sid,sname), not repeated in each enrollment.

topics.title: Third normal form
topics.definition: A relation is in 3NF when for every nontrivial X → A, X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute (part of some candidate key).
details: This condition removes problematic transitive dependencies while allowing some dependency-preserving designs that BCNF would split.
Always state the dependencies and candidate keys before claiming a normal form.
topics.example: If sid → dept and dept → office, then sid → office transitively. Store department office information in DEPARTMENT rather than repeating it for every student.

worked.title: Normalize enrollment records
worked.setup: ENROLLMENT(sid, sname, cid, title, grade), with key (sid,cid). Rules: sid→sname, cid→title, and sid,cid→grade.

steps.title: Check the values
steps.body: If each row has one sid, one cid, and one grade, it is atomic and meets 1NF. If courses were stored as a comma-separated list, first make one course per row.

steps.title: Remove partial dependencies
steps.body: sname depends only on sid; title depends only on cid. Split those facts into STUDENT(sid,sname) and COURSE(cid,title).

steps.title: Keep the full-key fact in enrollment
steps.body: grade depends on both sid and cid, so ENROLLMENT(sid,cid,grade) keeps it. The three relations reduce repeated names and titles.

worked.answer: STUDENT(sid,sname), COURSE(cid,title), and ENROLLMENT(sid,cid,grade) form a cleaner design. The key of ENROLLMENT is (sid,cid).

diagram.title: Move each fact to the table it depends on
diagram.caption: Student facts depend on sid, course facts on cid, and grades on both.

lessons.exam: Explain redundancy and all three anomalies. Normalize a relation step by step through 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF with the dependency removed at each step.

lessons.plain: BCNF checks every functional dependency: its left side must be a key. 4NF goes further and separates independent multi-valued facts.
goals: Show why 4NF can remove repeated combinations

topics.title: Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF)
topics.definition: A relation is in BCNF if, for every nontrivial functional dependency X → Y, X is a superkey.
details: A nontrivial dependency says the right side is not already part of the left side.
BCNF is stricter than 3NF. A BCNF decomposition is lossless when performed with the standard violating dependency, but it may not preserve every dependency locally.
topics.example: If instructor → course is a rule but instructor is not a key in a teaching-assignment relation, that dependency violates BCNF.

topics.title: Multivalued dependency
topics.definition: X ↠ Y means that for one X value, the set of Y values is independent of the remaining attributes.
details: This is different from X → Y: there may be several Y values for one X.
If hobbies and languages are independent for each student, storing both in one table creates every hobby-language pairing.
topics.example: A student with 2 hobbies and 3 languages can create 6 rows, even though the hobbies and languages are separate facts.

topics.title: Fourth normal form (4NF)
topics.definition: A relation is in 4NF when every nontrivial multivalued dependency has a superkey determinant.
details: 4NF separates independent sets into different relations so unrelated values are not cross-multiplied.
After splitting, a join can recreate the possible combinations without storing each combination redundantly.

worked.title: Separate hobbies from languages
worked.setup: Student 7 has hobbies chess and hiking, and speaks Tamil, English, and Hindi. The two lists are independent.

steps.title: Count the repeated combinations
steps.body: One combined table needs 2 × 3 = 6 rows: every hobby is paired with every language.

steps.title: Identify the independent facts
steps.body: The hobby list depends on the student. The language list also depends on the student, but neither list determines the other.

steps.title: Split the relation
steps.body: Store (7,chess), (7,hiking) in StudentHobby and (7,Tamil), (7,English), (7,Hindi) in StudentLanguage.

worked.answer: The split removes cross-product redundancy. The original combinations can still be generated by joining the two relations on sid.

diagram.title: Separate independent lists
diagram.caption: Keep each multi-valued fact in its own relation; join only when needed.

lessons.exam: Compare 3NF and BCNF. Define MVD and 4NF, then show a relation with independent multi-valued facts and its decomposition.

lessons.plain: Decomposition splits one relation into smaller relations. A good split lets us join the pieces back without inventing rows and keeps important rules checkable.
goals: Tell lossless join from dependency preservation
Explain the purpose of the chase/tableau

topics.title: Lossless-join decomposition
topics.definition: A decomposition is lossless if joining its pieces recreates exactly the valid rows of the original relation.
details: A lossy split can create spurious tuples—combinations that never existed—or lose the original connections.
For a binary split R1 and R2, a standard sufficient test is that the common attributes functionally determine all of R1 or all of R2.
topics.example: If R(A,B,C) is split into AB and AC, the common attribute A must determine B or determine C for this standard binary test.

topics.title: Dependency preservation
topics.definition: A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the rules projected onto the smaller relations still imply all the original dependencies.
details: When dependencies are preserved, each rule can be checked on a local table without joining several tables.
Losslessness and dependency preservation answer different questions; check both.
topics.example: If A→B remains entirely inside R1(A,B), the DBMS can enforce it there.

topics.title: Chase / tableau test
topics.definition: The chase is a table-based procedure that applies dependencies to rows of symbols to test whether a decomposition is lossless.
details: Give each decomposed relation a row with distinguished symbols for included attributes and unique symbols for missing attributes.
Apply dependencies to make agreeing determinant columns agree on dependent columns. If a row becomes all distinguished symbols, the decomposition is lossless.
topics.example: The chase is useful when there are more than two decomposed relations and the simple binary test is not enough.

topics.title: Problems caused by a poor decomposition
topics.definition: A decomposition can be harmful if joining the pieces invents rows or if important dependencies can no longer be checked locally.
details: A lossy decomposition produces spurious tuples: the join contains combinations that were not valid in the original relation.
A decomposition that is not dependency-preserving may require joins to enforce an original rule. This increases work and can let invalid states pass if checks are not coordinated.
Test both properties separately: losslessness protects reconstruction meaning; dependency preservation protects local rule checking.
topics.example: Suppose a relation records which student studies which subject with which instructor. A split that keeps only student-subject and student-instructor can recombine an instructor with a subject the student never took. The extra joined row is spurious.

worked.title: Test a binary decomposition
worked.setup: R(A,B,C) has dependency A→B. Decompose into R1(A,B) and R2(A,C).

steps.title: Find the common attributes
steps.body: R1 ∩ R2 = {A}. A is the overlap between the two decomposed relations.

steps.title: Check what the overlap determines
steps.body: By A→B, A determines both attributes of R1: A and B. Therefore the overlap determines one complete side.

steps.title: Check the dependency too
steps.body: A→B is contained in R1, so it can be enforced directly there. This split is lossless and preserves this dependency.

worked.answer: The natural join of R1(A,B) and R2(A,C) reconstructs R without spurious tuples, and A→B remains locally checkable.

diagram.title: Split, then join the pieces
diagram.caption: The shared key reconnects the two relations without adding false matches.

lessons.exam: Define lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition, apply the binary test, and explain what the chase/tableau establishes.
